A B S T R A C T
Coal mine accident information is typically fragmented and unstructured, limiting traditional methods in sys
tematic analysis and intelligent decision-making. To address this issue, this study presents a large language
model (LLM)-enhanced knowledge graph (KG) framework for coal mine accidents. An ontology covering 13
entity types and 8 relation types is designed to ensure standardized and extensible knowledge representation.
Accident reports are automatically collected, processed, and structured through LLM-based triple extraction. Key
elements such as accident type, location, time, level, and consequence are standardized and filtered to construct a
high-quality, multidimensional knowledge graph, stored in a Neo4i database for visualization and management.
The knowledge graph further supports interactive visualization and querying, enabling users to explore accident
entities, navigate relationships, and retrieve subgraphs related to specific hazards or accident types. Based on the
constructed KG, temporal-spatial-type analyses and FP-Growth-based association rule mining are conducted to
identify potential relationships and patterns among accident factors. The results demonstrate that the proposed
LLM-enhanced KG approach effectively improves accident data organization, semantic understanding, and
knowledge-driven analysis, providing a practical pathway toward digital and intelligent mine safety
management.

extraction of accident information from text [14–17]. For example, as
sociation rule mining and statistical learning methods have been used to
identify key risk factors and their interactions [14], while deep learning
models such as BERT have enabled accurate classification and cause

Knowledge graphs (KGs), as semantic network technologies for
organizing complex associative knowledge, have demonstrated strong
capabilities in knowledge modeling and reasoning across various do
mains, including railway systems [17], manufacturing [18], robotics
and aerospace engineering [19,20], and cybersecurity [21,22]. In the
coal mine safety domain, prior research has employed text mining and
complex network methods to construct accident causation networks
[11], multi-level accident analysis models [23], and multidimensional
statistical models [8–10,16], contributing to a more systematic under
standing of accident mechanisms. However, most existing approaches
rely heavily on rule-based extraction or task-specific supervised models,
which often require extensive manual annotation and exhibit limited
adaptability to complex semantics and large-scale accident corpora.
With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs) in
recent years, new opportunities have emerged for KG construction.
Recent transformer-based foundation models, such as GPT-series,
LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek [24], demonstrate strong generalization
and contextual reasoning capabilities, enabling them to handle complex
semantic understanding tasks beyond the scope of traditional NLP
models. A growing body of research has systematically investigated the
application of LLMs to knowledge-intensive tasks, including named
entity recognition, relation extraction, event extraction, and automatic
KG construction [18–22,25]. Compared with rule-based methods and
task-specific supervised models, LLMs show clear advantages in few-shot
or zero-shot learning scenarios and in processing long, unstructured
texts, thereby alleviating the dependence on large-scale labeled data and
handcrafted rules. Recent studies have further explored the integration
of LLMs with KGs, demonstrating that such hybrid approaches can
enhance both the automation and accuracy of knowledge acquisition as
well as reasoning performance in complex industrial contexts. Repre
sentative applications include industrial robot fault diagnosis [19],
aerospace assembly [23], and semantic parsing of coal mine accident
reports. For example, LLM-based data augmentation methods have
improved nested entity recognition and semantic extraction, while
combining KGs with LLMs has strengthened reasoning in complex in
dustrial environments [20]. In addition, frequent pattern mining
methods, such as FP-Growth and its improved variants, provide effective
tools for discovering risk patterns and supporting complex data mining
on structured knowledge representations [26–28]. Collectively, these
studies indicate that introducing LLMs into accident knowledge
extraction has significant potential to overcome the limitations of
traditional approaches and to enable efficient parsing and systematic
knowledge construction from large-scale accident texts.
Motivated by the above, this study addresses the challenges of
fragmented coal mine accident information, low levels of data struc
turing, and limited intelligent analysis capabilities. This paper proposes
an LLM-enhanced method for coal mine accident KG construction and
intelligent analysis. The main objective of this study is to construct a
large-scale, standardized, and knowledge-enhanced coal mine accident
knowledge graph and to demonstrate its effectiveness in supporting
multidimensional analysis and intelligent decision-making. Compared
with existing coal mine accident analysis and knowledge graph studies,
this work introduces several methodological and technical innovations.
The main contributions are as follows:
(1) This paper develops a domain-specific, standardized ontology-
based semantic framework for coal mine accidents, specifying
13 entity types and 8 relation types, thereby providing a unified
model for knowledge representation and integration.
(2) This paper applies an LLM-based approach to triple extraction
from accident texts, enabling efficient semantic parsing of
unstructured data and improving both the quality and efficiency
of knowledge acquisition compared with rule-based or traditional
NLP methods.
(3) This paper constructs a high-quality, large-scale, multidimen
sional coal mine accident knowledge base, stores it in a graph
database, and provides visualization functions, thereby providing
reliable data support for advanced analysis.
(4) This paper conducts knowledge-driven multidimensional statis
tical analyses and association rule mining based on the con
structed KG, revealing spatiotemporal accident patterns and
causal chain couplings, and providing quantitative insights for
risk warning and intelligent decision-making.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details
the ontology-based KG construction process, including semantic
ontology design, data acquisition, LLM-based triple extraction, and en
tity standardization. Section 3 presents intelligent analysis applications
of the KG, including multidimensional statistical analysis and associa
tion rule mining. Finally, Section 4 summarizes the research findings.
2. Knowledge graph construction for coal mine accidents
The methodological framework of this study consists of two major
components (see Fig. 1): the construction of a coal mine accident KG and
knowledge-graph-based intelligent analysis.
First, during the KG construction stage, a domain-specific ontology
model for coal mine accidents was designed, encompassing both entity
and relation schemas. Multi-source accident data were acquired and
preprocessed, and an LLM was employed to perform efficient triple
extraction. On this basis, key elements—including geographic locations,
accident times, accident types, accident levels, and accident con
sequences—were standardized and subjected to quality control,
ensuring the consistency and reliability of the graph data.
Second, in the intelligent analysis stage, multidimensional statistical
analyses and association rule mining were performed based on the
constructed knowledge graph, identifying spatiotemporal accident pat
terns and latent causal associations.

integrating professional knowledge of coal mine safety, regulatory

applications.

2.2. Data collection and triple extraction
High-quality domain-specific corpora serve as a fundamental basis
for constructing a coal mine accident KG. In this study, the official
website of the State Administration of Mine Safety (Coal Mine Safety
Network, https://www.mkaq.org) was selected as the primary data
source, and automated information collection and text processing
techniques were employed to systematically acquire historical coal mine
accident reports. The dataset spans from 1960 to 2025, comprising 4118
accident reports and covering most provinces and regions in China,
thereby providing strong spatiotemporal representativeness.
The collected unstructured accident texts contain critical informa
tion regarding the entire accident lifecycle, causal mechanisms,
responsible entities, and remedial actions. Traditional information
extraction approaches, which largely rely on rule-based methods or
conventional machine learning models, often exhibit limited general
ization when handling domain-specific terminology ambiguities, com
plex syntactic structures, and implicit semantic relations, thus
compromising the accuracy and comprehensiveness of triple extraction.
To address these challenges, this study introduces the Chinese LLM
DeepSeek R1 (https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1), com
bined with a predefined coal mine accident ontology template, to
implement an efficient triple-extraction pipeline tailored for this
domain.
Specifically, each accident text is concatenated with an ontology-
constrained prompt template and input into the DeepSeek model to
generate candidate triples via the API (see Fig. 3). Subsequently, the
output is parsed and structurally normalized using regular expressions,
eliminating non-compliant or semantically redundant entries. Each
extracted triple comprises the following fields: Accident ID, Head Name,
Head Label, Relation, Tail Name, and Tail Label, ensuring structural
consistency and domain conformity for the KG.
To quantitatively evaluate the proposed LLM-based triple extraction
framework, 17 representative Chinese coal mine accident reports were
manually annotated, yielding 191 ground-truth triples. The annotated
subset was selected to cover diverse accident types and narrative styles,
providing a focused yet representative evaluation of extraction perfor
mance. Precision, Recall, and F1-score were adopted as evaluation
metrics. To accommodate linguistic variability in accident narratives, a
fuzzy-matching evaluation strategy integrating entity similarity and
temporal tolerance was employed. As shown in Table 3, the DeepSeek-
based method consistently outperforms ChatGPT, achieving consis
tently higher recall without sacrificing precision. On average, 10–25
high-quality triples are extracted per report, effectively capturing acci
dent entities, causal relations, responsibility assignments, and mitiga
tion measures. DeepSeek-R1 was selected primarily due to its suitability
for Chinese coal mine accident narratives. As an open-source Chinese
large language model, DeepSeek-R1 enables reproducible, large-scale
processing of coal mine accident data while demonstrating strong
instruction-following capability and domain adaptability for ontology-
constrained structured extraction.

spans.content: 2.2. Data collection and triple extraction
High-quality domain-specific corpora serve as a fundamental basis
for constructing a coal mine accident KG. In this study, the official
website of the State Administration of Mine Safety (Coal Mine Safety
Network, https://www.mkaq.org) was selected as the primary data
source, and automated information collection and text processing
techniques were employed to systematically acquire historical coal mine
accident reports. The dataset spans from 1960 to 2025, comprising 4118
accident reports and covering most provinces and regions in China,
thereby providing strong spatiotemporal representativeness.
The collected unstructured accident texts contain critical informa
tion regarding the entire accident lifecycle, causal mechanisms,
responsible entities, and remedial actions. Traditional information
extraction approaches, which largely rely on rule-based methods or
conventional machine learning models, often exhibit limited general
ization when handling domain-specific terminology ambiguities, com
plex syntactic structures, and implicit semantic relations, thus
compromising the accuracy and comprehensiveness of triple extraction.
To address these challenges, this study introduces the Chinese LLM
DeepSeek R1 (https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1), com
bined with a predefined coal mine accident ontology template, to
implement an efficient triple-extraction pipeline tailored for this
domain.
Specifically, each accident text is concatenated with an ontology-
constrained prompt template and input into the DeepSeek model to
generate candidate triples via the API (see Fig. 3). Subsequently, the
output is parsed and structurally normalized using regular expressions,
eliminating non-compliant or semantically redundant entries. Each
extracted triple comprises the following fields: Accident ID, Head Name,
Head Label, Relation, Tail Name, and Tail Label, ensuring structural
consistency and domain conformity for the KG.
To quantitatively evaluate the proposed LLM-based triple extraction
framework, 17 representative Chinese coal mine accident reports were
manually annotated, yielding 191 ground-truth triples. The annotated
subset was selected to cover diverse accident types and narrative styles,
providing a focused yet representative evaluation of extraction perfor
mance. Precision, Recall, and F1-score were adopted as evaluation
metrics. To accommodate linguistic variability in accident narratives, a
fuzzy-matching evaluation strategy integrating entity similarity and
temporal tolerance was employed. As shown in Table 3, the DeepSeek-
based method consistently outperforms ChatGPT, achieving consis
tently higher recall without sacrificing precision. On average, 10–25
high-quality triples are extracted per report, effectively capturing acci
dent entities, causal relations, responsibility assignments, and mitiga
tion measures. DeepSeek-R1 was selected primarily due to its suitability
for Chinese coal mine accident narratives. As an open-source Chinese
large language model, DeepSeek-R1 enables reproducible, large-scale
processing of coal mine accident data while demonstrating strong
instruction-following capability and domain adaptability for ontology-
constrained structured extraction.
2.3. Entity standardization and quality control
To address potential inconsistencies, semantic deviations, and noise
introduced by LLMs during triple extraction, a systematic entity stan
dardization and quality control process was implemented to ensure both
structural consistency and semantic coherence of the extracted knowl
edge. This process comprises five key components:

2.3.1. Geographic location standardization
To ensure the consistency of spatial information, geographic loca
tions were standardized by mapping diverse expressions into a
normalized naming and hierarchical structure, thereby providing a
reliable basis for spatial analysis and cross-case comparison. All
geographic entities were unified using the format “Province (Munici
pality/Autonomous Region)–Mine,” with missing information repre
sented by “XX” (see Fig. 4).
The standardization procedure was implemented as follows:
Province and mine name available – Directly standardized to “Actual
Province–Actual Mine.”
Province only – Standardized to “Actual Province–XX Mine.”
Both province and mine names are missing – Unified as “XX Prov
ince–XX Mine.”
Mine name only – The missing province was supplemented using an
LLM. Using this strategy, provincial information for 265 accident re
cords lacking explicit province annotations was supplemented based on
contextual cues. The LLM-generated results were manually reviewed,
and no incorrect province assignments were identified.
If no explicit geographic location entity was present in the accident
text, the procedure further examined whether a mine location entity was
available. In such cases, a mapping between mine location and
geographic location was appended at the end of the record. If neither
entity was detected, the location was defaulted to “XX”.
2.3.2. Accident time standardization
To address the heterogeneity and occasional absence of accident
occurrence times, this study implemented a unified encoding and
correction procedure to ensure accuracy and comparability in statistical
analyses and temporal reasoning. Specifically, all accident times were
standardized into the format “YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss” (see Fig. 5). If
an accident time entity was present in the text, its conformity to the
standard format was first evaluated: non-standard representations were
converted using Python-based regular expression rules, while valid en
tries were retained without modification. In cases where no explicit
accident time entity was available, a supplementary triple was appended
at the end of the document in the form: “Accident Name (Entity) —
Accident Name — Occurred — XX-XX-XX XX:XX:XX — Accident Time”.
2.3.3. Accident filtering
To enhance the completeness and representativeness of the accident
corpus, a systematic filtering and correction process was implemented
on top of location and time normalization. This procedure removed
duplicate entries, records with missing critical attributes, and non-coal
mine accidents, thereby ensuring the retained data possessed high-
quality characteristics suitable for subsequent entity analysis and KG
construction. The process consisted of three main steps (see Fig. 6):
(1) Province and Time Filtering – Accident reports were examined for
completeness by extracting province information from location
entities and year–month–day information from time entities.
Records with more than one unknown attribute were deemed
incomplete and discarded.
(2) Duplicate Accident Removal – Using province and date attributes
as matching keys, pairwise comparisons were conducted, sup
plemented by manual verification, to eliminate duplicate entries.
(3) Non-Coal Accident Filtering – Accident names and other key at
tributes were analyzed with the aid of an LLM to determine
domain relevance, and non-coal mine incidents were excluded to
maintain dataset consistency with the research scope. Using this
strategy, 126 non-coal mining accident records were identified
and excluded from the dataset.
After applying these multi-stage filtering and correction procedures,
3035 valid accident reports were retained, forming a high-quality and
representative corpus to support subsequent analyses.

dent information within the KG, personnel casualties, economic losses,
and severity levels were standardized. First, accident consequences were
reformulated into four unified categories: “X fatalities”, “X serious in
juries”, “direct economic loss of X million CNY”, and “others”. The
processing workflow was as follows (see Fig. 7): if consequence infor

quence”. If consequence descriptions were present, the original ex
pressions were removed, standardized through an LLM, and represented

Accident consequence entity, Accident consequence”. Using this pro
cedure, a total of 2,936 non-standardized accident consequence ex
pressions were normalized by the LLM, among which 32 cases required
manual correction during the review process (approximately 1.1%).

This section leverages the statistical capabilities of the graph data
base to conduct multidimensional analyses of accident cases across

The temporal distribution of coal mine accidents and associated fa
talities is illustrated in Fig. 9. Overall, between 1960 and 2005, both the
number of accidents and the death tolls exhibited a sustained upward
trend. It should be noted, however, that underreporting, delayed
reporting, or incomplete records during this period may have led to an
underestimation of the actual risk levels. From 2005 to 2013, frequent
accidents coincided with persistently high fatality counts, reflecting the
heightened safety supervision pressures amid surging coal demand and
intensified mining activities. Since 2014, both accident occurrences and
fatalities have demonstrated a marked decline, closely linked to the
implementation of systematic safety reforms in China. Key regulatory
measures, including the revised Work Safety Law (2014) and the
Opinions on Further Strengthening Coal Mine Safety (State Council
Document No. 99, 2013), alongside policies targeting the closure of
small mines and the promotion of mechanization and informatization,
have strengthened the legal framework for coal mine safety and
enhanced accountability. Simultaneously, the adoption of intelligent
mining, real-time monitoring, early-warning systems, and emergency
response mechanisms has significantly reduced accident incidence and
fatalities. Collectively, these temporal trends reveal not only the his
torical evolution of coal mine accidents but also the critical roles of
legislation, policy enforcement, and technological advancements in
shaping risk trajectories.
Building on this temporal analysis, the spatiotemporal evolution of
coal mine accidents from 2005 to 2024 was further examined (see
Fig. 10). The distribution patterns indicate pronounced heterogeneity
across both time and space. Spatially, Inner Mongolia, Liaoning, Shanxi,
and Shaanxi provinces emerged as high-incidence regions, reflecting
their abundant coal resources, large-scale production, and dense mine
networks, which concentrate safety risks. Notably, in 2011, Inner
Mongolia recorded over 60 accidents, representing a historical peak,
largely attributable to robust coal market demand, large-scale mine
expansion, and relatively weak local supervision. Temporally, since
2014, accident counts in these major coal-producing regions have
decreased significantly, indicating the cumulative impact of national
safety regulations and industrial policies. It is important to note, how
ever, that the rate of decline varies across provinces, highlighting the
critical influence of local governance capacity, corporate safety in
vestments, and mining conditions on risk mitigation.

coal mine safety.

(a) Key findings from statistical analysis
In the temporal dimension, from 1960 to 2005, both accident fre
quency and fatalities exhibited a general upward trend, although early
underreporting and incomplete data likely underestimated actual risk
levels. Between 2005 and 2013, the indicators displayed a “high fre
quency—high volatility” pattern. Since 2014, both measures have
shown a marked decline, reflecting the synergistic governance effects of
strengthened legal frameworks, phasing out of outdated production
capacities, and the adoption of mechanization, informatization, and
intelligent mining technologies.
In the spatial dimension, provincial-level accident distributions
reveal pronounced heterogeneity. High-frequency provinces do not fully
coincide with high-fatality provinces, suggesting that geological
complexity, industry scale, governance capacity, and safety investment
jointly shape regional safety performance.
Regarding accident types, most categories have declined signifi
cantly since 2014, with M&E accidents exhibiting the most pronounced
reduction. However, water inrush accidents continue to show persis
tence and suddenness, reflecting the long-term challenges posed by
hydrogeological conditions under deep mining operations.
In terms of level, general, major, and particularly major accidents all
demonstrate overall downward trends, whereas relatively major acci
dents show relatively slower reduction, indicating that their causation is
more coupled and sudden, necessitating enhanced dynamic risk control
measures.
(b) Key patterns from data mining
Association rule mining using the FP-Growth algorithm revealed two
robust patterns:
“High-frequency—low-severity” cluster: M&E, transportation, roof
fall, and other accident types are strongly associated with general ac
cidents (e.g., M&E Accident → General Accident with confidence ≈
0.99, lift > 1), indicating that these events are primarily driven by
operational and equipment management factors and represent control
lable, low-to-moderate risk. While individual incident consequences are
limited, their cumulative effect and disruption to production remain
non-negligible.
“Low-frequency—high-severity” cluster: Gas-related accidents are
strongly linked to major and particularly major accidents and exhibit
regional clustering in high-gas provinces. This pattern highlights their
suddenness, systemic nature, and destructive potential, marking them as
the primary drivers of mass-casualty incidents.
The findings also have direct implications for accident prevention.
By leveraging the knowledge graph and the derived spatiotemporal and
association patterns, safety managers can pinpoint high-risk provinces,
accident types, and seasons, enabling focused safety inspections, pro
active control of severe accident drivers (e.g., gas-related hazards), and
evidence-based decision-making to improve mine safety.
